title: What to Bring to an IEP Meeting, and What to Have Already Written Down
description: IEP meetings are short, crowded, and scheduled around the school's calendar. What to prepare beforehand so the hour is spent on decisions rather than on reconstructing the year.
intro: An IEP meeting is usually an hour, sometimes less, with six or seven people around the table who have all read a document you may have received the night before.

The parents who get the most out of that hour are not the loudest or the most credentialed. They are the ones who walked in with the year already written down. Everyone else is working from memory, and memory loses to a printed log every time.
Nothing here is legal advice. It is preparation: what to gather, what to write down as the year happens, and what to ask for in the room.

sections.heading: Ask for the draft in advance
paragraphs: Request a copy of the draft IEP and any evaluations or progress reports before the meeting, in writing, and ask for them with enough time to actually read them. A few days is reasonable.
Reading a document for the first time while eight people wait is not a fair way to make decisions about your child, and asking for it early is an ordinary request rather than a confrontational one.
You are a member of the IEP team. That is the frame worth holding, and it is not adversarial. Most of these meetings go well, and preparation is what makes the difference in the ones that do not.

sections.heading: Bring the year, not your memory
paragraphs: This is the part that has to happen before the week of the meeting, because it cannot be reconstructed.
bullets: Progress reports, all of them, in date order. Goals are measured against these.
Your own log of what actually happened: the hard mornings, the refusals, the calls home, the good stretches and what was different about them.
Service minutes. What the IEP promised versus what was delivered. Missed sessions are common and rarely tracked by anyone but a parent.
Work samples, especially ones that show the gap between what the report says and what comes home.
Outside evaluations and provider notes — private therapy, medical, anything relevant.
Your email log. What you asked, when, and whether anyone answered. Unanswered requests carry weight only if they are documented.

sections.heading: Write down three things you want, before you go
paragraphs: Meetings drift. An hour disappears into a discussion of one accommodation and the thing that actually matters gets four minutes at the end while people are standing up.
Decide in advance what your three priorities are, in order, and write them on the top of your page. If you leave having covered those three, it was a good meeting, whatever else happened.

Frame each one around what you have observed rather than what you have concluded. "He is being denied support" invites a defence. "Here are eleven mornings in the log where he did not get into the building before 9:40, and here is what the aide told me" invites a plan.

sections.heading: Bring a second person
paragraphs: Two parents, a friend, a relative, or an advocate. One person listens and participates, the other writes.

It is very hard to do both while also being emotionally involved in the subject, and afterwards two people remember a meeting far better than one. If you plan to bring an advocate, tell the school in advance as a courtesy.

sections.heading: In the room
paragraphs: Take notes on decisions rather than on discussion. Who said what does not matter much. What was agreed, by whom, and by when is the whole record.
When something is agreed to, ask for it to be reflected in the document rather than in the conversation. A commitment that lives only in the minutes of a meeting is difficult to hold anyone to later.
It is fine to say you need time to think. You do not have to sign anything at the table, and asking for a day is normal.

Before people leave, ask two questions: what happens next and by when, and who is responsible for each item. Then send a short email afterwards summarizing what you understood was agreed. It is a courtesy, and it is also a dated record that exists whether or not anyone replies.

sections.heading: One thing that changed in 2026
paragraphs: Federal oversight of special education moved in June 2026. The Department of Education transferred responsibility to the Department of Health and Human Services, which now handles funding distribution and compliance monitoring, and to the Department of Justice, which handles civil rights complaints, a role previously held by the Education Department's Office for Civil Rights.
What did not change: IDEA is still federal law, IEPs are still required, and parent rights under IDEA are unchanged. Only Congress can alter that. Existing IEPs and 504 plans were not affected.

The practical consequence is narrow. If you ever need to file a federal civil rights complaint, the agency that receives it is different than it was. For everything that happens in the room, nothing has changed.

sections.heading: Then keep the log going
paragraphs: The meeting is one hour of a school year that is roughly a thousand hours long. What made it go well was the record you kept in the months before it.
Log as it happens, in one place, in short entries with dates. Ten seconds on the day beats an evening of reconstruction in April, and the difference shows up in the room.

faq.q: Can I ask for the draft IEP before the meeting?
faq.a: Yes, and it is worth doing in writing with a few days' notice. Reading a document for the first time while the team waits is not a reasonable way to make decisions. Ask for evaluations and progress reports at the same time.

faq.q: What should I bring to an IEP meeting?
faq.a: Progress reports in date order, your own log of what happened during the year, a comparison of service minutes promised against minutes delivered, work samples, any outside evaluations, and your email log including requests that were never answered. Also bring your top three priorities written down.

faq.q: Do I have to sign the IEP at the meeting?
faq.a: You can ask for time to review it rather than signing at the table. Taking a day to read it is a normal request. Before people leave, confirm what happens next, by when, and who is responsible, then send a short summary email as a dated record.

takeaway: The hour goes to whoever walked in with the year written down. Ask for the draft in advance, bring progress reports, your own log, and service minutes promised against delivered, decide your three priorities beforehand, and bring someone to take notes. Then confirm in writing what was agreed.
